lead: The impulse response h(t) is the output of an LTI system when the input is the unit impulse δ(t). The step response s(t) is the output when the input is the unit step u(t). These two signals describe the system completely: s(t) is the running integral of h(t), and h(t) is the derivative of s(t). Engineers measure them on filters, motors and circuits because one short test can predict the response to many inputs. The link is used in oscilloscope probing, control tuning and audio rooms.
prereq: You need Unit 1 standard signals δ(t) and u(t), and Chapter 2.1 on LTI systems.

sections.h3: Impulse response is the system fingerprint

blocks.text: An impulse is a very short input with unit area. Apply δ(t) to a continuous-time LTI system at rest. The output is h(t), the impulse response. Some syllabi call h(t) the weighting function because it tells how strongly an impulse at time zero affects the output at later times.

h(t) belongs to the system, not to the input. A causal system has h(t)=0 for negative t: it cannot answer before the impulse arrives. Because the system is time invariant, an impulse delayed to time t0 produces h(t−t0). This shift rule is the seed of the convolution integral.

The unit of h(t) comes from the system. For the RC low-pass below, h(t)=(1/τ)e<sup>−t/τ</sup>u(t) and the factor 1/τ has unit s<sup>−1</sup>. The factor sets both the height and the unit; dropping it gives a wrong number and a wrong dimension.
An LTI system is fully described by h(t). Once h(t) is known, every zero-state output follows from superposition. Causality and stability are also read from h(t).

sections.h3: Step response is the integral of h(t)

blocks.text: The step response s(t) is the output when the input is the unit step u(t), again from rest. Only a few books use the name indicial response for the same signal.
An impulse is the derivative of a step, so the step is the running integral of the impulse. For an LTI system:

blocks.where: s(t) is the step response, h(λ) is the impulse response at time λ, and λ is a dummy variable. The lower limit −∞ keeps any response before t=0.

blocks.text: For a causal system h(λ)=0 for negative λ, so s(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup> h(λ)dλ for t≥0. Differentiate the integral:

blocks.where: ds/dt is the slope of the step response. If s(t) jumps at t=0, the derivative adds an impulse at that instant; a continuous rise gives no impulse. Do not swap the two responses: s(t) is not h(t).

blocks.text: For the RC low-pass with τ=RC, h(t)=(1/τ)e−t/τu(t). Integrate from 0 to t: s(t)=(1−e−t/τ)u(t). The capacitor voltage starts at 0, reaches 63.2% of its final value at t=τ, 95.0% at 3τ, and 99.3% at 5τ. The differential-equation route to the same result is in Section 2.6.

The figure plots the same RC filter against t/τ. The falling curve is τh(t)=e<sup>−t/τ</sup>; the rising curve is s(t)=1−e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. At t/τ=0, τh=1 and s=0. At t/τ=1, τh=e<sup>−1</sup>=0.368 and s=1−e<sup>−1</sup>=0.632. At t/τ=5, s=0.993, so the response is settled for most engineering work.
Notice the slopes. The slope of s(t) at any time equals h(t). A large h means a fast rise; a small h means a slow rise. This is why h(t) is the derivative of s(t) and s(t) is the integral of h(t).

On a lab bench, a narrow pulse approximates δ(t), and a square wave with a long period gives repeated step inputs. The two measurements must agree through the integral and derivative relations. If they do not, check the time constant, the load resistance, and the probe capacitance.

figure.caption: Normalised RC low-pass responses against t/τ. At t/τ=1 the step response is 0.632 and the scaled impulse response is 0.368.

spec.aria: Normalised impulse response falls from one while the step response rises from zero to one, both plotted against t over the time constant.

examples.question: An RC low-pass filter has R=1 kΩ and C=1 μF. The output is the capacitor voltage. Find τ, h(t), s(t), and their values at t=1 ms.
steps: For this first-order low-pass, h(t)=(1/τ)e<sup>−t/τ</sup>u(t). Substitute τ=0.001 s: h(t)=(1/0.001)e<sup>−t/0.001</sup>u(t)=1000 e<sup>−1000t</sup>u(t) s<sup>−1</sup>.
examples.answer: τ=1 ms; h(t)=1000e<sup>−1000t</sup>u(t) s<sup>−1</sup>; s(t)=(1−e<sup>−1000t</sup>)u(t); at t=1 ms, h=368 s<sup>−1</sup> and s=0.632.
examples.check:
import math
R = 1e3
C = 1e-6
tau = R * C
h0 = 1 / tau
t = 1e-3
s_t = 1 - math.exp(-t / tau)
h_t = h0 * math.exp(-t / tau)
print(f'{tau:.3f}')
print(f'{h0:.1f}')
print(f'{s_t:.3f}')
print(f'{h_t:.0f}')

traps: Swapping h(t) and s(t): h(t) is the impulse response and s(t)=∫h; the step response is not the derivative of the impulse response.
Dropping u(t) and assuming the formula holds for all time: a causal RC filter has h(t)=0 and s(t)=0 for negative t.
Losing the 1/τ in h(t): for R=1 kΩ and C=1 μF, h(0)=1000 s<sup>−1</sup>, not 1.
Differentiating e<sup>−t/τ</sup> as −e<sup>−t/τ</sup>: the chain rule gives h(t)=(1/τ)e<sup>−t/τ</sup>u(t), with the positive 1/τ.
Treating δ(t) as an ordinary finite pulse: the ideal impulse has unit area and zero width; a real pulse only approximates it if its width is much smaller than τ.

quiz.q: Define h(t) and s(t) for a continuous-time LTI system at rest.
quiz.a: h(t) is the output for input δ(t); s(t) is the output for input u(t).

quiz.q: Why is s(t) the integral of h(t)?
quiz.a: A unit step is a sum of shifted impulses from −∞ to t; by LTI superposition the output is the sum, which becomes the integral.

quiz.q: An RC low-pass has τ=2 ms. Find h(0) and s(τ).
For h(t)=3e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t) s<sup>−1</sup>, find s(t) and s(0.5 s).

quiz.a: Another name for the step response s(t).

quiz.q: What does h(t)=0 for negative t say about the system?
quiz.a: The system is causal: output cannot start before the input impulse.
h(t)=ds/dt=5e<sup>−5t</sup>u(t) s<sup>−1</sup>; s is continuous at 0, so no impulse term.

beyond: Not for the exam. System identification estimates h(t) from measured input-output records by deconvolution, then predicts responses to new inputs; oscilloscope step response is a daily check for probes and cables. In control, h(t) and s(t) guide tuning and stability margins, while room impulse responses drive audio reverberation and echo effects. Search terms: impulse response measurement, step response time constant, deconvolution, system identification.
